Today's work practices that skill with specific evidence and structural explanation."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"routine","definition":"a regular, usual way of doing things","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"suckered","definition":"tricked or fooled into doing or believing something (informal)","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"rebellious","definition":"refusing to obey rules or authority","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"resented","definition":"felt angry or bitter about something unfair","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"regretted","definition":"felt sorry about something that happened or that one did","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"muzzle","definition":"the nose and mouth of an animal such as a horse or dog","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"desperate","definition":"feeling or showing a strong need to act because the situation seems hopeless","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"bellow","definition":"to shout or roar in a loud, deep voice","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"cloven","definition":"split into two parts, like the hoof of a goat","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"hooves","definition":"the hard coverings on the feet of animals such as horses and goats","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"turning point","definition":"the moment in a story when events change direction and a character cannot go back to the way things were","tier":"support"},{"word":"climax","definition":"the most intense moment in a plot, when the main conflict peaks","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 37–43"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate what they know about Percy's ordinary world and think about how one event can change everything for a character.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"When Ordinary Life Suddenly Changes","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.5"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with your partner. What was it like after?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What makes a moment a turning point instead of just another event?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A turning point is when something happens that you can't undo. Like when Harry Potter finds out he's a wizard, his normal life with the Dursleys is over and a new one starts."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In Chapter 3, Percy's field trip, his school life and his home life all collide in one stormy afternoon. Today we read pp. 37–43 to see how this moment closes Percy's ordinary world and starts his adventure. As you read, keep our question in mind: What fears and values about family are reflected on these pages?"},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. Take two or three quick shares, then move on. Students will revisit the idea of a turning point in Learning in Action."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students learn ten vocabulary words in context, using word parts and context clues, and look at vowel teams and prefixes while adding the words to their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers.","activities":[{"id":"lab-vocab-context-clues","title":"Vocabulary in Context: Meaning, Word Parts and Sound Patterns","minutes":10,"standards":["L.6.4"],"routine":"Introduce New Words Using Context and Word Parts","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 37–43"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Target words by page: routine (p. 37), suckered (p. 38), rebellious (p. 38), resented (p. 39), regretted (p. 39), muzzle (p. 41), desperate (p. 42), bellow (p. 42), cloven (p. 43), hooves (p. 43). Teach in three quick clusters so the ten words fit in ten minutes. Students need their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Cluster 1, the feelings words: resented and regretted. Write both words. Say: Both start with the prefix re-, which often means again or back. But in resented and regretted the re- is part of the root, so we can't peel it off the way we can in redo. Notice that the words are about looking back at something that already happened. Read the sentence around each word on p. 39 and decide what each feeling is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using the sentence on p. 39, what is the difference between resented and regretted?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Resented means being angry or bitter about something unfair, like when someone feels another person got a better deal. Regretted means feeling sorry about something you did or that happened. Resent is anger at someone, regret is sorry about it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Cluster 2, the character and situation words: routine, suckered, rebellious, desperate. Have students find each word on its page and underline the clues. For routine, look for words about doing the same thing every day. For suckered, ask whether the word sounds formal or like how kids really talk. That informal tone tells us about the narrator, Percy. For rebellious, notice the root *rebel* and the suffix *-ious*, meaning full of or having the quality of. For desperate on p. 42, ask what the characters are doing that shows they are out of options."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What clues in the text help you figure out what rebellious means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The word rebel is inside it, and the text describes someone who breaks the rules and doesn't listen to teachers. So rebellious means acting against rules and the people in charge."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Cluster 3, the sound-and-sight words: muzzle, bellow, cloven, hooves. Write bellow and hooves. Point out the vowel teams: in bellow, the letters ow make the long o sound, /ō/; in hooves, the letters oo make the /oo/ sound, as in moon. Have students say both aloud twice. Then connect meaning: a muzzle is an animal's nose and mouth, cloven means split in two, and hooves are an animal's hard feet. Ask students to picture what creature those three words describe together."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which words in this cluster help you picture the creature, and what do they tell you about it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Muzzle, cloven and hooves all help me picture an animal. Cloven hooves are split in two like a goat's, so the creature is part goat. Bellow tells me it makes a loud, deep roar."},{"type":"directions","text":"Add all ten words to your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer. For each word, write the page number, a definition in your own words, and one clue from the text. For bellow and hooves, underline the vowel team. For resented and regretted, circle the prefix re-."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Words like suckered and bellow are informal or vivid. Point out that Riordan's choice of these words gives Percy's narration a real, kid-like voice. This supports RL.6.4 and L.6.5 work later in the unit."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Using context to determine word meaning","tryThis":"Have students read the whole sentence aloud, cover the word, and say what would make sense in the blank. Then give two choices and ask which fits better. Provide a sentence frame: I think ___ means ___ because the text says ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Word meaning and word choice","tryThis":"Ask students to compare desperate with a similar word such as nervous and explain how the stronger word changes the mood of the scene. Have them find another word in pp. 37–43 that signals Percy's voice."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students read pp. 37–43 closely and cite key events and reactions to track the turning point. Part B: Students analyze how this episode fits into the plot structure, closing Percy's ordinary world and launching the adventure, and connect it to fears and values about family.","activities":[{"id":"lia-track-turning-point","title":"Part A: Track the Turning Point","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.1","L.6.4"],"routine":"Close Read & Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 37–43"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we read the storm, the monster attack and Grover's reveal as one chain of events. Our job is to find the exact moments where things change and to cite them. Remember, a strong citation names what the text says and explains what it shows."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 37–43 and complete a three-column chart. Column 1: Key event (storm, monster attack, Grover's reveal). Column 2: Evidence (a short quote or paraphrase with the page number). Column 3: Reaction (how Percy, Grover or others respond, and what that shows). Annotate with a star (★) next to the moment you think is the turning point."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details on pp. 37–38 show that the day started as part of Percy's usual routine, and what warning signs show up?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On p. 37 the class is on a normal field trip, with Percy's usual pattern of trouble and being the outsider. Then on p. 38 things start to feel off, like the storm and the odd behavior of people around him. Those are warnings that his ordinary world is about to break."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How do Percy and the others react during the monster attack on pp. 41–42? Cite a specific detail."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On p. 42 Percy feels desperate, and the text shows him struggling to protect himself and Grover. The detail that a creature can bellow shows it is huge and dangerous. Percy doesn't run away. He fights, which shows he is braver than he thinks."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Grover's reveal on p. 43 show about him, and why does it change how Percy sees his world?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"On p. 43 the text describes cloven hooves, so Grover is not a normal kid. He was hiding the truth, so Percy realizes the people he trusted aren't what they seemed. His ordinary world isn't real anymore."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which family fears and values show up on these pages, for example in how Percy thinks about his mom or his past?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy fears that he is disappointing his mom or being a burden, and he resented how he's treated. But he also values protecting the people close to him, like Grover and his mom. That shows family matters to him even when he's afraid."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and citing evidence about events and reactions. Language focus: precise verbs for reactions and sequence words.","sayAsk":"Have students say each event aloud with a partner before writing it. Ask: What happens first? Then what? How does Percy react? Provide frames: First, ___ happens on page ___. Percy reacts by ___. This shows that ___. Encourage adverbials: Percy moves quickly toward Grover. Suddenly, the storm gets worse. Rephrase a student's short answer: You said Percy was scared. We can say, Percy reacts fearfully when the creature bellows on page 42.","watchFor":"If students retell the whole story without citing, then prompt: Which exact line shows that? Give me the page number. If students list events without reactions, then prompt: How did the character respond? Success: students name an event, cite a detail with a page number, and explain what the reaction shows."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.5"],"stem":"Which detail from pp. 37–43 most strongly signals that Percy's ordinary world is ending?","choices":[{"text":"Percy goes on a field trip with his class.","correct":false,"rationale":"This shows Percy's ordinary routine at the start of the chapter, not the moment it ends."},{"text":"Grover is revealed to have cloven hooves, showing he is not who Percy thought.","correct":true,"rationale":"This reveal proves the world is not what Percy believed, so he cannot return to his normal life."},{"text":"Percy feels regretted about something he did earlier.","correct":false,"rationale":"Regret is a feeling in the chapter, but it does not by itself end Percy's ordinary life. It's a reaction, not the turning point."},{"text":"The class takes a break from the field trip.","correct":false,"rationale":"This is a minor, ordinary detail that doesn't change the direction of the plot."}]},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Citing evidence for events and reactions","tryThis":"Give a partially filled chart with page numbers already listed. Have students find and copy the matching line, then complete the sentence: On page ___, the text says ___, which shows ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Evaluating the strongest evidence","tryThis":"Ask students to rank the three events by how much each changes Percy's life, and defend the ranking with two quotes. Have them decide whether the turning point is one moment or a chain of moments."}]}]},{"id":"lia-explain-plot-structure","title":"Part B: Explain the Turning Point in the Plot Structure","minutes":15,"standards":["RL.6.5","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 37–43"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A story's plot has parts: exposition (the ordinary world and characters), rising action (problems build), climax or turning point (the big change), and what follows. A chapter fits into this structure by doing a job. Chapters 1 through 3 so far showed Percy's ordinary world and its troubles. This episode does a new job: it closes that world and launches the adventure. We explain that by saying what came before, what changes, and what it makes possible."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Model: In pp. 37–43, the storm, the monster attack and Grover's reveal work together as a turning point. Before this episode, Percy's ordinary world is school troubles and a hard home life. Because the creature attacks and Grover shows his cloven hooves, Percy learns that monsters are real. As a result, he can't go back to normal, and the adventure begins."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy's ordinary world look like before this episode, and how do you know?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Before this, Percy is a kid who gets in trouble at school and worries about his mom and Gabe. The earlier chapters, like Chapter 3's start, show him dealing with normal problems, not monsters."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this episode launch the adventure? What can Percy no longer do?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It launches the adventure because Percy now knows monsters are real and that he is part of something bigger. He can't go back to pretending everything is normal, so he has to go forward."},{"type":"directions","text":"Write a 4–5 sentence paragraph explaining how the storm, the monster attack and Grover's reveal on pp. 37–43 close Percy's ordinary world and launch the adventure. Use at least two cited details from your chart. Include at least two adverbials that add detail about time, place, manner or cause (for example: during the storm, suddenly, because of the attack, with desperate effort). Connect to the essential question by mentioning one fear or value about family."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"Sentence starters: This episode is a turning point because ___. Before it, Percy ___. During the storm, ___ (page ___). Because ___, Percy ___. As a result, the adventure ___."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining a text's structure and in adding detail with adverbials. Language focus: sequence and cause-effect connectors and adverbials of time, place, manner and cause.","sayAsk":"Have students rehearse aloud with a partner first. Say: Tell your partner what happened before, during and after. Provide frames: Before this episode, ___. During the storm, ___. Because of the attack, ___. As a result, ___. Model expanding a simple sentence: Percy fights. Percy fights bravely near the bus during the attack because he wants to protect Grover. Invite students to plan in a shared home language, then write in English.","watchFor":"If students write only a retelling, then prompt: How does this episode change what comes next? If students use no adverbials, then prompt: Add when, where, how or why to this sentence. Success: students state what the ordinary world was, what changes, and what the change launches, with at least two cited details and added adverbials."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Explaining structure","tryThis":"Give a before/after t-chart with two headings, Ordinary world and New world. Have students fill in one detail for each, then turn the two details into one sentence with because or so."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Plot structure and theme","tryThis":"Ask students to explain how this episode also develops a theme about family and protection, and to find one earlier moment (Lessons 7–8) that this turning point echoes or reverses."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students summarize the turning point and its impact on Percy, and connect it to the Performance Task skill.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-reflect","title":"Reflect: A Turning Point and Its Impact","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.5"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"shared","text":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, you will trace a turning point in a plot and explain its impact on a character. Today you practiced exactly that with Percy."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the template: The turning point on pp. 37–43 is ___. Before it, Percy's world was ___. After it, Percy ___. One fear or value about family shown in these pages is ___."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The turning point on pp. 37–43 is when Grover's cloven hooves show that monsters are real. Before it, Percy's world was school troubles and a hard home life. After it, Percy has to leave his ordinary life behind and start an adventure. One value about family shown in these pages is that Percy wants to protect the people he cares about, like Grover and his mom."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Collect the templates as an exit check. Look for a named event, a before/after contrast, and a family fear or value. Use what you see to plan small groups for Lesson 10."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Students preview Chapter 4 and prepare to analyze how the truth is revealed.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch4","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 4","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1","RL.6.10"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 44–50"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read and annotate Chapter 4 (pp. 44–50).
